claim: Active vision is well-documented across species.
source: Active vision, the sensory-motor process through which animals dynamically adjust visual input to sample and prioritise relevant information via photoreceptors, eyes, head, and body movements, is well-documented across species.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of research on active vision across species.

claim: In small-brained animals like insects, where parallel processing may be limited, active vision for sequential acquisition of visual features might be even more important.
source: In small-brained animals like insects, where parallel processing may be limited, active vision for sequential acquisition of visual features might be even more important.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the importance of active vision in insects based on their brain size and processing capabilities.

claim: Bumblebees tended to inspect only a small region of each pattern, with a preference for lower and left-side sections.
source: We observed that bees tended to inspect only a small region of each pattern, with a preference for lower and left-side sections, before accurately accepting target or rejecting distractor patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and data analysis of bee flight paths.

claim: The specific pattern areas scanned differed between the plus and multiplication signs.
source: The specific pattern areas scanned differed between the plus and multiplication signs, yet flight behaviour remained consistent and specific to each pattern, regardless of whether the pattern was rewarding or punishing.
evidence: This is based on observational data from the experiments.

claim: Flight behaviour remained consistent and specific to each pattern, regardless of whether the pattern was rewarding or punishing.
source: The specific pattern areas scanned differed between the plus and multiplication signs, yet flight behaviour remained consistent and specific to each pattern, regardless of whether the pattern was rewarding or punishing.
evidence: This is based on observational data from the experiments.

claim: Bees could generalise their pattern recognition to partial cues in transfer tests.
source: Transfer tests showed that bees could generalise their pattern recognition to partial cues, maintaining scanning strategies and selective attention to learned regions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transfer tests.

claim: Bees maintained scanning strategies and selective attention to learned regions during transfer tests.
source: Transfer tests showed that bees could generalise their pattern recognition to partial cues, maintaining scanning strategies and selective attention to learned regions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transfer tests.

claim: Active vision is a crucial aspect of bumblebees' visual processing.
source: These findings highlight active vision as a crucial aspect of bumblebees' visual processing, where selective scanning behaviours during flight enhance discrimination accuracy and enable efficient environmental analysis and visual encoding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Selective scanning behaviours during flight enhance discrimination accuracy in bumblebees.
source: These findings highlight active vision as a crucial aspect of bumblebees' visual processing, where selective scanning behaviours during flight enhance discrimination accuracy and enable efficient environmental analysis and visual encoding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In vertebrates, active vision strategies include large-scale movement by the body or head, or smaller scale movements of the eyes (saccades) or photoreceptors.
source: To scan visual targets, there can be large-scale movement by the body or head, or smaller scale movements of the eyes (saccades) or photoreceptors (Juusola and Song, 2017; Najemnik and Geisler, 2005; Yang and Chiao, 2016) as well as subtle head movements or head-bobbing, which induce motion parallax to assess distances (Dutta et al., 2020; Dutta and Maor, 2007; Kral, 2003; Kral, 1998; Sobel, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Subtle head movements or head-bobbing induce motion parallax to assess distances in vertebrates.
source: To scan visual targets, there can be large-scale movement by the body or head, or smaller scale movements of the eyes (saccades) or photoreceptors (Juusola and Song, 2017; Najemnik and Geisler, 2005; Yang and Chiao, 2016) as well as subtle head movements or head-bobbing, which induce motion parallax to assess distances (Dutta et al., 2020; Dutta and Maor, 2007; Kral, 2003; Kral, 1998; Sobel, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Active vision is essential for obtaining an accurate three-dimensional representation of the surrounding environment.
source: Such active vision is essential for obtaining an accurate three-dimensional representation of the surrounding environment (Kagan, 2012; Kemppainen et al., 2022; Martinez-Conde et al., 2013; Martinez-Conde and Macknik, 2008; Werner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In certain vertebrates, eye movements are used as a sampling strategy, enhancing the encoding of high spatial frequency of natural stimuli and providing fine spatial information.
source: In certain vertebrates, eye movements are also used as a sampling strategy, enhancing the encoding of high spatial frequency of natural stimuli and providing fine spatial information (Anderson et al., 2020; ; Kuang et al., 2012; Rucci and Poletti, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some animals adopt characteristic routes during visual tasks to facilitate target recognition.
source: Some animals adopt characteristic routes during visual tasks to facilitate target recognition (Skorupski and Chittka, 2017; Dawkins and Woodington, 2000; Langridge et al., 2021; Lehrer et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Individual chickens exhibit stereotyped approach paths when learning to discriminate visual patterns, consistently using the same path and side relative to the object during each trial.
source: For instance, individual chickens exhibit stereotyped approach paths when learning to discriminate visual patterns, consistently using the same path and side relative to the object during each trial (Dawkins and Woodington, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Chickens' approach paths are not identical across all chickens, as each bird develops its own distinct approach strategy.
source: However, these paths are not identical across all chickens, as each bird develops its own distinct approach strategy.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research on chickens.

claim: Chickens fail at visual discrimination tasks when their developed route is disrupted.
source: Interestingly, they fail at these tasks when their developed route is disrupted.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research on chickens.

claim: Characteristic head movements have been observed in pigeons during image stabilisation for forward locomotion.
source: Additionally, characteristic head movements have been observed in pigeons during image stabilisation for forward locomotion (Theunissen and Troje, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In bumblebees, complex patterns cannot be discriminated when they are only briefly flashed on a screen, preventing bees from sampling in a continuous scan.
source: Indeed, in bumblebees, there is evidence that complex patterns cannot be discriminated when they are only briefly flashed on a screen, preventing bees from sampling in a continuous scan (Nityananda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bumblebees' approach direction prior to landing affects their colour learning.
source: Langridge et al., 2021 explored how bumblebees' approach direction prior to landing affects their colour learning, showing that bees tend to remember the colour they predominantly face during their approach, which influences their learned preferences for floral patterns.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bees tend to remember the colour they predominantly face during their approach, which influences their learned preferences for floral patterns.
source: Langridge et al., 2021 explored how bumblebees' approach direction prior to landing affects their colour learning, showing that bees tend to remember the colour they predominantly face during their approach, which influences their learned preferences for floral patterns.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bees exhibit defined sequences of body movements in response to particular visual stimuli.
source: Furthermore, bees exhibit defined sequences of body movements in response to particular visual stimuli (Collett et al., 1993; Guiraud et al., 2018; Lehrer, 1994; MaBouDi et al., 2020a; MaBouDi et al., 2020b; Werner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The deterministic relationship between movement and perception suggests that active vision allows movement to shape the sensory information acquired and influences perception.
source: This deterministic relationship between movement and perception suggests that active vision allows movement to shape the sensory information acquired and influences perception.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited research.

claim: Bees are capable of memorising and discriminating a wide variety of visual patterns, including complex ones.
source: Extensive studies have demonstrated that bees are capable of memorising and discriminating a wide variety of visual patterns, including complex ones that, for example, include different stripe orientations in each of four quadrants (Avarguès-Weber et al., 2011; Benard et al., 2006; Dyer et al., 2005; Guiraud et al., 2025a; Srinivasan, 2010; Srinivasan, 1994; Stach et al., 2004; Turner, 1911; Frisch, 1914; Wehner, 1967).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is a long history of claims that bees are incapable of discriminating some relatively simple patterns.
source: On the other hand, there is a long history of claims that bees are incapable of discriminating some relatively simple patterns (Avarguès-Weber et al., 2011; Guiraud et al., 2022; Hertz, 1935; Hertz, 1929; Horridge, 1996; Srinivasan, 1994; Frisch, 1914).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Honeybees (Apis mellifera) were not able to distinguish a plus pattern from the same pattern rotated through 45° (multiplication sign pattern) in a Y-maze setup where the patterns were displayed at a fixed distance from the bees' decision point.
source: As one example, it was reported that honeybees (Apis mellifera) were not able to distinguish a "plus pattern", made up of a vertical and horizontal bar, from the same pattern rotated through 45° that is multiplication sign pattern (Horridge, 1996; Srinivasan et al., 1994) in a Y-maze setup where the patterns were displayed at a fixed distance from the bees' decision point.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The successes and failures of bees in discriminating visual patterns are not strictly related to pattern complexity.
source: However, there is evidence that the successes and failures of bees in discriminating visual patterns are not strictly related to pattern complexity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited research.

claim: The angle subtended on the visual field of a stimulus from a distance may limit the ability of bees to solve a specific task.
source: Factors such as the angle subtended on the visual field of a stimulus from a distance (Horridge, 1996; Srinivasan, 2010) and the particular sensitivity of orientation and colour selective neurons in the bee visual system (Paulk et al., 2009; Paulk et al., 2008; Roper et al., 2017; Maddess and Yang, 1997) may limit the ability of bees to solve a specific task.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The particular sensitivity of orientation and colour selective neurons in the bee visual system may limit the ability of bees to solve a specific task.
source: Factors such as the angle subtended on the visual field of a stimulus from a distance (Horridge, 1996; Srinivasan, 2010) and the particular sensitivity of orientation and colour selective neurons in the bee visual system (Paulk et al., 2009; Paulk et al., 2008; Roper et al., 2017; Maddess and Yang, 1997) may limit the ability of bees to solve a specific task.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The visual scanning procedures that bees use when examining and memorising patterns can affect performance.
source: Indeed, the visual scanning procedures that bees use when examining and memorising the patterns can also affect performance (Giurfa et al., 1999; Guiraud et al., 2025b; Lehrer, 1994; MaBouDi et al., 2023; Stach and Giurfa, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Forty bumblebees (Bombus terrestris audax) from six colonies were used in this study.
source: Forty bumblebees (Bombus terrestris audax) from six colonies were utilised and housed in wooden nest boxes connected to a flight arena (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and subjects.

claim: Two groups of bees (n=20 each) were trained using a differential conditioning protocol.
source: Two groups of bees (n=20 each) were trained using a differential conditioning protocol: one group was trained to associate the plus pattern with a reward (sucrose solution) while avoiding the multiplication pattern associated with punishment (quinine solution), and the other group was trained on the reciprocal arrangement (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: One group was trained to associate the plus pattern with a reward (sucrose solution) while avoiding the multiplication pattern associated with punishment (quinine solution).
source: Two groups of bees (n=20 each) were trained using a differential conditioning protocol: one group was trained to associate the plus pattern with a reward (sucrose solution) while avoiding the multiplication pattern associated with punishment (quinine solution), and the other group was trained on the reciprocal arrangement (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The other group was trained on the reciprocal arrangement.
source: Two groups of bees (n=20 each) were trained using a differential conditioning protocol: one group was trained to associate the plus pattern with a reward (sucrose solution) while avoiding the multiplication pattern associated with punishment (quinine solution), and the other group was trained on the reciprocal arrangement (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: After five bouts of training or upon reaching 80% performance in the last 10 choices, the bees underwent one learning test and three transfer tests.
source: After five bouts of training or upon reaching 80% performance in the last 10 choices, the bees underwent one learning test and three transfer tests.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Bees in Group 1 recognised the plus patterns as rewarding above chance after just 20 choices.
source: Bees in Group 1 recognised the plus patterns as rewarding above chance after just 20 choices (Figure 1C; Wilcoxon signed rank test; z=1.95, n=20, p=0.04; mean = 57%).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Group 2 achieved above-chance performance on the multiplication patterns after 30 choices.
source: Conversely, Group 2 achieved the same performance on the multiplication patterns after 30 choices (Wilcoxon signed rank test; z=2.34 n=20, p=3.6e-3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no notable difference in the learning rate between the two groups after 30 choices.
source: Nevertheless, there was no notable difference in the learning rate between the two groups after 30 choices (p=0.77), and the bees' performance was not affected by colony membership (p=0.25; Figure 1C; see Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The bees' performance was not affected by colony membership.
source: Nevertheless, there was no notable difference in the learning rate between the two groups after 30 choices (p=0.77), and the bees' performance was not affected by colony membership (p=0.25; Figure 1C; see Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: All bees achieved ≥92% (±7.8 SEM) correct choice performance after 70 choices of training.
source: The bees continued to increase in performance during the 70 choices of the training (per block of 10 choices, see Figure 1C); whereupon all bees achieved ≥92% (±7.8 SEM) correct choice performance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Both groups of bees had learned to select the rewarding patterns significantly above chance (>50%) after training.
source: The results of a generalised linear mixed model (GLMM) analysis confirmed that both groups of bees had learned to select the rewarding patterns significantly above chance (>50%) after training (Figure 1C, p=4.8e-9).
evidence: This is supported by GLMM statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Both groups of trained bees successfully learned to discriminate the plus from the multiplication sign, and vice versa, in the learning tests.
source: Additionally, the bees' performance in the learning tests indicated that both groups of trained bees successfully learned to discriminate the plus from the multiplication sign, and vice versa (Figure 1D; Wilcoxon signed rank test; z=3.21, n=13, p=1.3e-3 for Group 1; z=3.08, n=12, p=2.0e-3 for Group 2); again there was no significant difference between the performance of two groups in the learning test (Wilcoxon rank sum test; z=0.45, n=25, p=0.64).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There was no significant difference between the performance of two groups in the learning test.
source: Additionally, the bees' performance in the learning tests indicated that both groups of trained bees successfully learned to discriminate the plus from the multiplication sign, and vice versa (Figure 1D; Wilcoxon signed rank test; z=3.21, n=13, p=1.3e-3 for Group 1; z=3.08, n=12, p=2.0e-3 for Group 2); again there was no significant difference between the performance of two groups in the learning test (Wilcoxon rank sum test; z=0.45, n=25, p=0.64).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The bees' performance in the learning test was similar to that seen during the last block of 10 choices of the training phase.
source: The bees' performance in the learning test was similar to that seen during the last block of 10 choices of the training phase (Wilcoxon signed rank test z=1.09, n=25, p=0.27).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: For 8 out of the 13 bees in Group 1 (trained to plus) the first pattern to be inspected was the rewarding plus pattern.
source: During the learning tests, for 8 out of the 13 bees in Group 1 (trained to plus) the first pattern to be inspected (flight within 12 cm diameter of centre of pattern and 10 cm out from rear stimulus wall) was the rewarding plus pattern (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on observational data from the experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 5 out of the 12 bees in Group 2 also inspected one of the plus patterns first, in their case the incorrect pattern.
source: However, 5 out of the 12 bees in Group 2 also inspected one of the plus patterns first, in their case the incorrect pattern.
evidence: This is based on observational data from the experiments.

claim: The bees' pattern selection from a distance was no different to chance (50% correct initial pattern inspections).
source: Therefore, as a whole, the bees' pattern selection from a distance (i.e. from arena entrance to stimuli wall) was no different to chance (50% correct initial pattern inspections; Figure 1E; χ2 test, Chi-square statistics = 0.35, p=0.55).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: During all the correct initial inspections of both groups, the bees still scanned the pattern before flying to the feeder tube.
source: In addition, during all the correct initial inspections of both groups, the bees still scanned the pattern before flying to the feeder tube, further suggesting that the bees do not receive sufficient evidence for a choice from a distance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on observational data from the experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bees do not receive sufficient evidence for a choice from a distance.
source: In addition, during all the correct initial inspections of both groups, the bees still scanned the pattern before flying to the feeder tube, further suggesting that the bees do not receive sufficient evidence for a choice from a distance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on observational data.

claim: In the bottom-half test, bees demonstrated a statistically significant ability to discriminate between the bottom portions of the correct and incorrect patterns.
source: In the bottom-half test, bees demonstrated a statistically significant ability to discriminate between the bottom portions of the correct and incorrect patterns (Figure 2A; Wilcoxon signed rank test; z=2.81, n=10, p=4.9e-3 for Group 1; z=2.66, n=10, p=7.7e-3 for Group 2), suggesting that they could generalise their learned associations to these bottom cues.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Bees could generalise their learned associations to bottom cues.
source: In the bottom-half test, bees demonstrated a statistically significant ability to discriminate between the bottom portions of the correct and incorrect patterns (Figure 2A; Wilcoxon signed rank test; z=2.81, n=10, p=4.9e-3 for Group 1; z=2.66, n=10, p=7.7e-3 for Group 2), suggesting that they could generalise their learned associations to these bottom cues.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data.

claim: In the top-half test, bees exposed only to the upper sections of the patterns showed no significant preference for the correct pattern.
source: In contrast, the top-half test revealed that bees exposed only to the upper sections of the patterns showed no significant preference for the correct pattern (Figure 2B; Wilcoxon signed rank test; z=0.17, n=10, p=0.83 for Group 1; z=0.17, n=10, p=0.85 for Group 2), indicating that these cues alone were insufficient for discrimination.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Top-half cues alone were insufficient for discrimination.
source: In contrast, the top-half test revealed that bees exposed only to the upper sections of the patterns showed no significant preference for the correct pattern (Figure 2B; Wilcoxon signed rank test; z=0.17, n=10, p=0.83 for Group 1; z=0.17, n=10, p=0.85 for Group 2), indicating that these cues alone were insufficient for discrimination.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data.

claim: The single-bar orientation test showed a significantly higher response to bars matching the rewarded orientation across both groups.
source: The single-bar orientation test showed a significantly higher response to bars matching the rewarded orientation across both groups (Figure 2C; Wilcoxon signed rank test; z=2.70, n=10, p=6.8e-3 for Group 1; z=2.6, n=10, p=9.3e-3 for Group 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Bees trained to the plus pattern favoured the vertical bar.
source: Furthermore, bees trained to the plus pattern favoured the vertical bar, while those trained to the multiplication pattern showed an equal preference for the 45° and –45° bars, indicating orientation-specific associations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Kruskal-Wallis test; Chi-sq=25.72; df = 39, p=1.0e-5 for Group 1; Chi-sq=19.0; df = 39, p=3.0e-4 for Group 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bees trained to the multiplication pattern showed an equal preference for the 45° and –45° bars.
source: Furthermore, bees trained to the plus pattern favoured the vertical bar, while those trained to the multiplication pattern showed an equal preference for the 45° and –45° bars, indicating orientation-specific associations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Kruskal-Wallis test; Chi-sq=25.72; df = 39, p=1.0e-5 for Group 1; Chi-sq=19.0; df = 39, p=3.0e-4 for Group 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bees exhibited orientation-specific associations.
source: Furthermore, bees trained to the plus pattern favoured the vertical bar, while those trained to the multiplication pattern showed an equal preference for the 45° and –45° bars, indicating orientation-specific associations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Kruskal-Wallis test; Chi-sq=25.72; df = 39, p=1.0e-5 for Group 1; Chi-sq=19.0; df = 39, p=3.0e-4 for Group 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data.

claim: Bumblebees rely on specific parts of the visual patterns—particularly the lower sections—and individual bar orientations to recognise the overall pattern.
source: These results suggest that bumblebees rely on specific parts of the visual patterns—particularly the lower sections—and individual bar orientations to recognise the overall pattern.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: Bees may focus on a discriminable local feature of a pattern that suffices for recognition, while disregarding other elements.
source: This finding implies that bees may focus on a discriminable local feature of a pattern that suffices for recognition, while disregarding other elements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: The bees' initial flight speed upon entering the flight arena and approaching the first inspected stimulus was on median 0.20 (±0.13 SEM) m/s.
source: The bees' initial flight speed upon entering the flight arena and approaching the first inspected stimulus was on median 0.20 (±0.13 SEM) m/s (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The speed reduced to a median of 0.11 (±0.10 SEM) m/s whilst inspecting the stimulus.
source: The speed reduced to a median of 0.11 (±0.10 SEM) m/s whilst inspecting the stimulus; the highest proportion of flight speeds was less than 0.1 m/s (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The bees' speed increased to a median of 0.20 (±0.24 SEM) m/s whilst traversing between the presented patterns.
source: The bees' speed increased to a median of 0.20 (±0.24 SEM) m/s whilst traversing between the presented patterns (i.e. flights between the ⌀12cm x 10cm cylinder regions surrounding stimuli).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data.

claim: Bees typically scanned the patterns from a distance of 10 mm to 50mm from the stimuli.
source: Bees typically scanned the patterns (inspections with the lower flight speed of 0.20 (±0.13SEM) m/s) from a distance of 10 mm to 50mm from the stimuli (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The bees spent approximately 1.51 (±0.50 SEM) seconds inspecting a stimulus, irrespective of whether this was a plus sign or multiplication sign, or the correct or incorrect pattern.
source: The bees spent approximately 1.51 (±0.50 SEM) seconds inspecting a stimulus, irrespective of whether this was a plus sign or multiplication sign, or the correct or incorrect pattern (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The flight speed during inspection when rejecting a pattern was on average three times that of when the bee accepted a pattern and flew to the feeder.
source: The flight speed during inspection when rejecting a pattern was on average three times that of when the bee accepted a pattern and flew to the feeder (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The bees showed an overall tendency to scan the patterns with their bodies oriented at ~±30° relative to the rear stimuli wall, keeping one or other eye predominantly aligned to the stimuli during the scans.
source: Interestingly, the bees showed an overall tendency to scan the patterns with their bodies oriented at ~±30° relative to the rear stimuli wall, keeping one or other eye predominantly aligned to the stimuli during the scans (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: When flying between the patterns, bees mostly looked forward in the direction of their motion with a much wider range of flight directions relative to the rear wall.
source: Conversely, when flying between the patterns, they mostly looked forward in the direction of their motion with a much wider range of flight directions relative to the rear wall (see Discussion section).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data.

claim: In most instances (Group 1 trained to ⊕: 89.2%, Group 2 trained to ⊗: 87%), the bees first traversed to, and then scanned, the lower part of the patterns regardless of whether the target was rewarding or aversive.
source: In most instances (Group 1 trained to ⊕: 89.2%, Group 2 trained to ⊗: 87%), the bees first traversed to, and then scanned, the lower part of the patterns regardless of whether the target was rewarding or aversive (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In Group 1, the bees scanned the bottom centre before deciding to land in 54% of all correct choices.
source: In Group 1, the bees scanned the bottom centre before deciding to land in 54% of all correct choices.
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Group 2, the bees accurately rejected the patterns, and the bottom centre was scanned prior to their rejection in 39.7% of instances.
source: In Group 2, the bees accurately rejected the patterns, and the bottom centre was scanned prior to their rejection in 39.7% of instances.
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data.

claim: The bees consistently displayed a preference for the lower left corner.
source: It is crucial to emphasise that the bees consistently displayed a preference for the lower left corner, which will be further discussed in the subsequent analysis.
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data.

claim: Bees trained on the protocol with the plus pattern as rewarding (Group 1) would typically approach the lower half of the stimulus (89% of inspections).
source: Bees trained on the protocol with the plus pattern as rewarding (Group 1) would typically approach the lower half of the stimulus (89% of inspections).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data.

claim: Group 1 bees would scan the lower centre of the pattern (containing the vertical bar) and then fly directly to the pattern centre to access the feeding tube.
source: They would scan the lower centre of the pattern (containing the vertical bar) and then fly directly to the pattern centre to access the feeding tube (Figure 4A and E, see Video 2).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4A and E, and Video 2.

claim: If Group 1 bees observed a multiplication sign, they would usually scan the lower left corner of the pattern, containing the +45°-angled bar of the multiplication sign.
source: However, if the bees observed a multiplication sign, they would usually scan the lower left corner of the pattern, containing the +45°-angled bar of the multiplication sign (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Over half of Group 1 trials consisted of a single corner scan before the bees rejected the patterns.
source: Of these trials, over half consisted of a single corner scan before the bees rejected the patterns.
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data.

claim: The inspection of a single diagonal pattern element was sufficient to ascertain that the pattern was not a plus sign.
source: A scan of the whole pattern was clearly not required: the inspection of a single diagonal pattern element was sufficient to ascertain that the pattern was not a plus sign.
evidence: This is an inference based on video analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the remaining cases the bees would traverse to the opposite lower corner, then scan the remaining oriented bar before rejection.
source: In the remaining cases the bees would traverse to the opposite lower corner, then scan the remaining oriented bar before rejection (Figures 3F and 4A).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 3F and 4A.

claim: On average, in only 4.5% of such inspections did the bees only scan the right corner.
source: On average, in only 4.5% of such inspections did the bees only scan the right corner.
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data.

claim: If Group 2 bees were inspecting a multiplication sign stimulus, they would first approach the left or right lower section of the pattern.
source: If the bees were inspecting a multiplication sign stimulus, they would first approach the left or right lower section of the pattern (Figure 4C and E, see Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C and E, and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: Group 2 bees showed the same preference for the left-side inspections, double that of the lower right-side scans.
source: We still observed the same preference for the left-side inspections, double that of the lower right-side scans.
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were far fewer instances of Group 2 bees inspecting both corners before flying to the feeding tube.
source: However, there were far fewer instances of bees inspecting both corners before flying to the feeding tube (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: When Group 2 bees (trained to the multiplication pattern) encountered a plus pattern they would again scan the lower centre at the base of the vertical bar.
source: When Group 2 bees (trained to the multiplication pattern) encountered a plus pattern they would again scan the lower centre at the base of the vertical bar (see Video 3).
evidence: This is based on video analysis of experimental data shown in Video 3.

claim: Group 2 bees would also, on occasion, scan the lower left corner where no oriented bar was present.
source: In contrast to the Group 1 bees accepting the multiplication symbol, these bees would also, on occasion, scan the lower left corner where no oriented bar was present (Figure 4C).
